title: Four Quiet Ways a Fortune Fails
summary: Personal wealth is rarely destroyed by one bad investment. It is destroyed by four structural faults: currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan. Each looks harmless in good years, and in a crisis they tend to arrive together.
body:
A fortune does not usually fail in one dramatic loss. It fails through four structural faults that sit quietly on the balance sheet for years: currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan. Find them in a calm year, because a crisis reveals them all at once.

Recall

Q. In personal tax planning, what is the basic trade-off between taking salary and taking dividends from a company you own?

A. Salary is usually deductible to the company and taxed as employment income to you, and it can build entitlements tied to earned income. Dividends come from after-tax corporate profit and are taxed differently in your hands. The right mix depends on the rules where you live; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is an investment policy statement?

A. A written document that sets the objectives, risk limits, asset ranges, liquidity needs and reporting rules for a pool of wealth, so that every adviser works to the same instructions and every decision can be tested against them.

Q. What does key-person insurance protect?

A. The business, not the family. It pays the company if a person whose skills or relationships the business depends on dies or becomes disabled, buying time to replace them or to meet lender conditions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the third of our post-mortem weeks, and Roman joins me because personal wealth is judged the way a lender judges a project: not by how good the upside looks, but by what happens on the worst day. You are building wealth through development, which means large, illiquid, leveraged positions, often across borders. That profile is exactly where the four quiet faults live. A developer can do every project well and still lose the family's security because of how the wealth around the projects was arranged.

The four faults, in plain English

First, currency mismatch: your assets earn or are valued in one currency while your debts or your spending are in another. If the two currencies move apart, your net worth moves even though nothing about the buildings changed.

Second, concentration: too much of your net worth sits in one asset, one market, one tenant, one partner or one bank. Concentration is how fortunes are built, and it is also how they are lost, because there is nothing else to absorb a fall.

Third, custody: who actually holds your assets and keeps the records of what you own. If the person who invests your money also holds it and also produces the statements, you are trusting one party to tell the truth about itself.

Fourth, no estate plan: no current will, no powers of attorney, no record of where things are and who decides. The wealth survives you, but control over it passes to a court process and to people you did not choose.

The professional framing is that these are not investment risks. They are architecture risks. An investment risk is the chance a building underperforms. An architecture risk is the chance that the way you hold everything turns an ordinary setback into a permanent loss. Weeks 85 to 95 built the architecture. This week tests it to failure.

Why they arrive together

In a calm year these four faults look unrelated. In a crisis they become correlated. A currency falls when a local economy weakens. The same weakness lowers local property values and tightens local credit. A fraudulent manager is most likely to be exposed when markets fall and investors ask for their money back. And the year of greatest stress is often the year a founder falls ill, because stress and long hours are not good for anyone. Check the health side of that with your doctor; the financial side is ours.

Here is the first worked example, using hypothetical round numbers. A developer holds 10,000,000 dollars of assets. 8,000,000 dollars is property in one city. 1,000,000 dollars is cash in a local bank. 1,000,000 dollars is a managed account. He owes 4,000,000 dollars, borrowed in a currency different from the one his rents are paid in. Net worth is 6,000,000 dollars.

Now a single regional shock. Local property falls 25 percent: 8,000,000 becomes 6,000,000, a loss of 2,000,000. The rent currency falls 20 percent against the loan currency, so the debt, measured in the rent currency, rises from 4,000,000 to 5,000,000, a further loss of 1,000,000. The local bank restricts withdrawals for a period, so the 1,000,000 of cash is present on paper but not usable. Net worth on paper falls from 6,000,000 to 3,000,000, half gone, and usable liquidity falls to whatever the managed account will release. One shock, three faults, and the developer's liquidity floor has vanished in the same month his lender wants more equity.

Say that out loud now.

In a crisis, my risks stop being separate. Plan for them to arrive together.

Roman's lens: reading a personal balance sheet like a lender

Roman's practice is to ask four questions of any balance sheet, including yours. What currency is each line in, and what currency do I spend? What share of the whole is the single largest exposure? Who holds each asset, and can I confirm its existence from someone other than the person who manages it? If I died tonight, who would have legal authority over each line tomorrow morning?

Second worked example. A hypothetical balance sheet of 5,000,000 dollars net worth. Roman lists it in a table and adds four columns: currency, share of total, holder and successor. The table immediately shows that 60 percent is one project company, that the managed account is held by an affiliate of the adviser, and that the successor column for the project shares is blank because the shareholders' agreement is silent and there is no will. Nothing has gone wrong. But three of the four faults are visible in ten minutes, and each has a known control.

FaultThe control
Currency mismatchMatch debt and reserves to the currency of income and spending
ConcentrationA written maximum share for any single exposure
CustodyIndependent custodian, administrator and auditor
No estate planCurrent wills, powers of attorney and an asset map

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not any one fault. It is believing that because each fault is small on a normal day, the combination is small on a bad one. The control is a single annual stress test of the whole personal balance sheet, run with all four faults switched on at once, and a written trigger: if the severe case breaches your liquidity floor, you act before the next deal, not after it. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any specific change.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats wealth protection as something to do after he is wealthy. In reality, the faults are cheapest to fix when the numbers are small, the structures are new and nobody is yet under pressure. A will costs far less than an intestate estate. Matching a loan to the right currency is a choice at term-sheet stage; unwinding it later is a refinancing.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax: currency gains and losses, and the way assets pass at death, can each carry tax consequences; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the holding structure decides which creditors can reach which assets in a crisis. Banking: a second banking relationship in a second jurisdiction is a liquidity control, not a luxury. Governance: someone must have authority to act if you cannot, written down in advance. Estate: the asset map and the wills must describe the same assets. Exit: a concentrated position is only worth its paper value if there is a buyer when you need one.

Callback

In week 43, Roman taught country risk: currency mismatch, convertibility and transfer risk at the level of a project. This week takes the same ideas home. A project that borrows in a currency it does not earn carries a hedge or a reserve. Your personal balance sheet deserves the same discipline, because nobody is monitoring it for you.

Recap

Wealth fails through architecture more often than through investments. The four quiet faults are currency mismatch, concentration, custody and no estate plan; they become correlated in a crisis, so test them together, once a year, with written triggers.

Next: Ford, with Roman assisting, on Failure Forensics: the Madoff fraud and what custody really means.
checklist: I can list every asset and debt by currency, and the currency I spend.
I know my single largest exposure as a share of net worth.
I have written a maximum share for any one exposure.
I can confirm each investment account from an independent custodian.
I have a current will and powers of attorney where I hold assets.
I keep an asset map that names a successor for each line.
I run one combined stress test a year with all four faults switched on.
I have a written trigger that tells me when to act.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, wealth rarely dies from one bad investment. It dies from four structural faults. Currency mismatch: assets in one currency, debts or spending in another. Concentration: too much in one asset, market, partner or bank. Custody: the same person invests your money, holds it and reports on it. And no estate plan: no will, no powers of attorney, no map of who decides. On a calm day each fault looks small. In a crisis they arrive together, because the same shock that drops a currency also drops local property, tightens local banks and exposes a weak manager. So I read my own balance sheet the way a lender would: currency, share of total, holder and successor for every line. Once a year I stress all four faults at once, against a written liquidity floor, and I act before the next deal if the floor breaks. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Currency mismatch — holding assets or income in one currency while debts or spending are in another, so exchange-rate moves change net worth.
Concentration — a large share of net worth in a single asset, market, counterparty or institution.
Custody — the safekeeping of assets and the official record of who owns them, held by a custodian.

hostile.q: Your projects all perform, so why should I care how your personal wealth is arranged?
hostile.a: Because a personal crisis becomes a project crisis. If my currency, concentration, custody or estate arrangements failed in the same downturn that tested your loan, I could not inject equity or honour a guarantee. So I test my personal balance sheet with all four faults switched on, I keep a liquidity floor in the currency of my obligations, and I can show you the custodian confirmations and the summary of my estate documents.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman (Risk and the lender's view)
title: Madoff: When the Manager Also Held the Money
summary: Bernard Madoff ran the largest known Ponzi scheme, exposed in December 2008. It survived for decades because one firm managed the money, held the money and produced the statements, and investors accepted smooth returns they could not verify. We take it through seven steps and end with a custody rule.
body:
The Madoff fraud lasted for decades because investors let one firm invest their money, hold their money and tell them what their money was worth. Separate those three jobs and a fraud of that kind cannot hide for long.

Recall

Q. What is a registered retirement or tax-sheltered account, in concept?

A. An account the tax law treats specially, usually deferring or exempting tax on growth in exchange for limits on contributions and withdrawals. The rules differ by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. In a family office, why should reporting be consolidated?

A. So that every account, entity and adviser is seen on one page, in one currency, on one date. Without consolidation, concentration and duplication hide between separate statements.

Q. What is disability insurance meant to replace?

A. Income lost when you cannot work because of illness or injury. For a founder whose income depends on personal effort, it is often the coverage people forget.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this case is a lesson in two places at once. It is a lesson in custody, which is the plumbing of personal wealth. And it is a lesson in concentration, because the people who were ruined were those who had put most of what they owned in one place. You will one day hand money to managers, funds and partners. This case tells you which questions to ask before you do.

The facts here are drawn from the public record. Where I am not certain of a detail, I describe it without a number.

1. Timeline

Bernard Madoff founded his securities firm in New York in 1960, and over the following decades it became a well-known trading firm. Alongside it ran an investment advisory business that reported remarkably steady returns, with very few losing months. Many clients reached him through feeder funds, which pooled outside money and passed it to Madoff. From 2000 onward, a financial analyst named Harry Markopolos repeatedly told the United States Securities and Exchange Commission that the returns were impossible, including a detailed written submission in 2005. Examinations took place and did not stop the fraud. In late 2008, as markets fell, clients asked for withdrawals the scheme could not meet. Madoff told family members it was a fraud, they reported him, and he was arrested on December 11, 2008. He pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years in prison. A court-appointed trustee spent years recovering money for victims. Losses reported on clients' statements ran to tens of billions of dollars.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions by investors mattered. First, accepting that Madoff's own firm would hold the securities and clear the trades, rather than an independent custodian. Second, accepting account statements produced by the same firm that managed the money. Third, for many feeder funds and their investors, accepting a very small accounting firm as auditor of a business that claimed to manage enormous sums.

3. Assumptions

Investors assumed that a famous, regulated, long-established firm could not be a fraud. They assumed that someone else, a regulator, a feeder fund or an auditor, had checked. They assumed that steady returns meant skill rather than a warning sign. And they assumed that a paper statement listing trades meant the trades had happened.

4. Incentives

The feeder funds earned fees on the money they passed in, so their incentive was to keep it flowing, not to question it. Early investors who received steady payouts had no reason to complain. The secrecy Madoff insisted on was presented as protecting a clever strategy, which made questions feel rude. The incentive for every individual to ask hard questions was weaker than the social pressure not to.

Say that out loud now.

If one firm invests my money, holds it and reports on it, I am trusting it to audit itself.

5. Warning signs ignored

Returns that were too smooth for the markets they claimed to trade. A strategy that, as analysts pointed out, would have required trading volumes the options markets could not support. Self-custody. A tiny auditor. Secrecy about how the money was made. Paper statements rather than independent electronic confirmation. Any one of these deserves a question. Together they were a pattern.

6. Point of no return

For each investor, the point of no return was the moment their money entered an arrangement where nobody independent could confirm it existed. After that, the only protection was that new money would keep arriving. When the 2008 crisis turned inflows into withdrawals, the scheme had no assets to meet them.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not one dishonest man. Fraud is a constant. The root cause was a structure that removed every independent check. When the manager, the custodian and the record-keeper are the same party, there is no second set of books, so a lie cannot be caught by comparison.

Roman's view: concentration turned fraud into ruin

Roman's point is that fraud explains the loss, but concentration explains the ruin. An investor with 5 percent of net worth in the scheme suffered a painful loss. An investor with 80 percent lost his home, his retirement and his ability to help his family.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. Two investors each have 4,000,000 dollars. The first puts 200,000 dollars, 5 percent, with a single manager; the second puts 3,200,000 dollars, 80 percent. The manager turns out to be a fraud and the money is gone, subject to whatever a trustee later recovers. The first investor falls from 4,000,000 to 3,800,000 dollars and keeps every part of his life. The second falls from 4,000,000 to 800,000 dollars, and if he had borrowed against the rest, possibly lower. Same fraud. The concentration decided the outcome.

A second example on the custody check. Suppose you hold a 1,000,000 dollar managed account. Under a separated structure, the manager places trades, an independent custodian holds the securities in your name and sends its own statement, and an independent administrator values the account. At quarter end you compare the manager's report with the custodian's statement. If the manager says 1,000,000 and the custodian says 600,000, you have found a 400,000 dollar problem in one comparison. Under self-custody there is only one statement, so there is nothing to compare.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reputation substituting for verification. A famous name, a respected friend who invested, or a long record makes people stop asking. The control is to insist, in writing, on independent custody, independent administration and a recognised independent auditor, and to confirm holdings directly with the custodian yourself at least once a year.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks steady returns are the good news. Markets are not steady. A return stream with almost no bad months is a reason to ask more questions, not fewer. The second beginner's mistake is being embarrassed to ask. A legitimate manager answers custody questions every week and is not offended by them.

Callback

In week 87, Warrick taught that fees and conflicts of interest are part of any investment's true cost. Madoff is the extreme case of an undisclosed conflict: the person reporting the value had every reason to report it falsely. And in week 72, REGA taught that know-your-customer works in both directions. You should know your manager as thoroughly as your bank knows you.

The prevention rule

Rule 96: Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties I can verify myself.

Recap

Madoff ran a fraud for decades because one firm managed, held and reported the money, and investors accepted smooth returns and a famous name in place of independent checks. Concentration turned the fraud into ruin for those who had put most of their wealth with him.

Next: Roman, on The Money: how currency mismatch and concentration move a personal balance sheet.
checklist: I know the name of the custodian for every account I hold.
Each custodian sends statements directly to me, not through the manager.
I compare the manager's report with the custodian's statement every quarter.
I know who audits each fund I invest in and whether that firm is recognised.
I treat unusually smooth returns as a reason to ask more questions.
No single manager holds more than my written maximum share of net worth.
I confirm holdings directly with each custodian at least once a year.
I am not embarrassed to ask any manager about custody.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, Bernard Madoff ran a fraud for decades and was arrested in December 2008. It survived because one firm invested the money, held the money and produced the statements, so there was never a second set of books to compare against. Investors accepted smooth returns, a famous name, a tiny auditor and secrecy, and assumed somebody else had checked. Analysts had warned regulators for years. When the 2008 crisis turned inflows into withdrawals, there was nothing behind the statements. Roman's point is that the fraud explains the loss, but concentration explains the ruin: an investor with 5 percent there was hurt, one with 80 percent lost everything. So my rule is this. Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties, and I confirm my holdings with the custodian myself.
terms: Ponzi scheme — a fraud that pays earlier investors with money from later investors rather than from real returns.
Feeder fund — a fund that pools outside investors' money and passes it to another manager to invest.
Independent administrator — a third party that values a fund's assets and keeps its records separately from the manager.

hostile.q: The manager has a twenty-year record and your friends all invest with him. Why are you insisting on an independent custodian?
hostile.a: Because a record and a reputation are not evidence that the assets exist. An independent custodian holding the securities in my name, sending me its own statement, is evidence. If the manager is legitimate, this costs him nothing; it is how institutional money is held every day. If he refuses, that refusal is the most important thing I will learn about him.

rule: Rule 96: Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties I can verify myself.

title: What a Currency Move and a Concentrated Bet Do to Net Worth
summary: Currency mismatch and concentration do not change the buildings; they change what the buildings are worth to you. Leverage multiplies both. This lesson prices them on a hypothetical personal balance sheet and shows the controls that keep a bad year survivable.
body:
A currency move and a concentrated bet can halve your net worth without a single tenant leaving. Leverage multiplies both, so the first question about any personal balance sheet is not how large it is, but how much of it would survive one bad year.

Recall

Q. Why does retirement income planning care about the order of withdrawals?

A. Because different accounts and assets can be taxed differently when money comes out, so the sequence changes the after-tax income for the same total. The rules are jurisdiction-specific; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What should a family office report every quarter?

A. Consolidated net worth by entity and asset class, performance against the investment policy statement, liquidity against the floor, fees paid, and any breach of the agreed limits.

Q. Why is the right amount of life insurance tied to debts and dependants rather than to net worth?

A. Because its job is to cover what would be owed and what dependants would need if you died, especially guarantees and loans that would otherwise force a sale of assets at a bad time.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer's personal balance sheet is unusual. It is large on paper, illiquid in practice, leveraged, and often spread across currencies. That combination means small percentage moves in a market or an exchange rate become large moves in your equity. Lenders price this when they look at a guarantor. You should price it before they do.

Currency mismatch, priced

In plain English: if you own something valued in one currency and owe money in another, your net worth now depends on the exchange rate as well as on the asset.

The professional framing is to measure net worth in the currency you spend, which is called your reporting currency, and to treat every asset and liability in another currency as an open position. The position is the asset value less the debt in that same currency. A net long position gains when that currency rises and loses when it falls.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. You spend in currency H. You own a building valued at 20,000,000 units of currency F, and today 1 F buys 1 H, so it is worth 20,000,000 H. You financed it with a 12,000,000 H loan. Net worth in this line is 8,000,000 H. Now currency F falls 25 percent: 1 F buys 0.75 H. The building is still 20,000,000 F, but it is now worth 15,000,000 H. The debt is still 12,000,000 H. Net worth falls to 3,000,000 H, a fall of 62.5 percent from a 25 percent currency move.

Change one thing. Borrow the 12,000,000 in currency F instead. After the same 25 percent fall, the building is 15,000,000 H and the debt is 9,000,000 H. Net worth is 6,000,000 H, a fall of 25 percent. Matching the debt to the asset's currency cut the loss from 5,000,000 H to 2,000,000 H. That is why a lender asks what currency the rent is paid in before it agrees the currency of the loan.

Say that out loud now.

Leverage turns a currency move into a much larger move in my equity. Match the debt to the income.

Concentration, priced

In plain English: the more of your wealth sits in one place, the more one bad event can take.

The professional framing is a concentration ratio, the largest single exposure divided by total assets, read together with leverage. The ratio alone is not enough. A concentrated, unlevered position can fall and recover. A concentrated, levered position can fall to the point where the lender forces a sale at the bottom, and then it never recovers.

Worked example two. Total assets 10,000,000 dollars, debt 5,000,000 dollars, equity 5,000,000 dollars. Of the assets, 8,000,000 is property in one market and 2,000,000 is spread across other holdings. The single market falls 30 percent. The property loses 2,400,000. Equity falls to 2,600,000, down 48 percent. Now reverse it: if only 4,000,000 had been in that market and 6,000,000 spread elsewhere, the same 30 percent fall costs 1,200,000 and equity falls 24 percent, assuming the other holdings held their value. In a real crisis they may not, because correlations rise, so Roman always runs a second case where everything falls together, just less.

The concentration nobody counts

Concentration is not only about assets. It is also about counterparties: the institutions and people your wealth depends on. If every account, every project loan and every deposit sits with one bank, that bank is a single exposure even though your balance sheet shows many lines. If one partner is in every deal, his insolvency, death or divorce touches all of them at once. If one tenant pays most of your rent, the tenant is the asset.

Roman adds a column to the balance sheet for this. Beside each line he writes the counterparty it depends on, then totals by counterparty. In a hypothetical example, a developer with 12,000,000 dollars of assets across nine lines discovers that 9,000,000 of it depends on one bank, either as depositor, borrower or account holder. No single line looked large. The total was 75 percent. The control is the same written limit, applied to counterparties as well as to assets, and a second banking relationship opened while nobody needs it.

How the best do it

Well-run institutional investors, such as large university endowments and pension funds, tend to share three habits a small developer can copy. They set written exposure limits by asset, market and manager, and they report against those limits every quarter rather than only when something breaks. They hold liquidity and hedges in the currency of their future obligations, so a currency move does not force them to sell assets to pay bills. And they separate the people who choose investments from the people who hold and value them. None of this needs a large staff; it needs a page of written limits and the discipline to read the report.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick's entry for this subject has three lines. First, record your net worth in your reporting currency and also as a currency table: how much is in each currency, net of debt in that currency. Second, record your concentration ratio, the largest single exposure as a share of total assets, beside your total personal leverage. Third, record the result of a combined stress case: a 30 percent fall in your largest market at the same time as a 20 percent fall in its currency. If that case leaves you below your liquidity floor, the ledger shows a gap you need to close. A licensed adviser is required before you act on hedging, refinancing or selling.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring net worth in the asset's currency and feeling safe. A building that holds its local value can still be a disaster in the currency your family spends. The control is to report net worth in one currency, monthly or quarterly, with the currency table attached, and to treat any net open position above your written limit as a decision to make, not a fact to live with.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hedges the asset and forgets the reserves. He matches the project loan to the rent currency, then holds the family's emergency cash in the same currency as the project. When that currency falls, the reserve falls with the asset, exactly when it is needed. Reserves should be held in the currency of the obligations they are meant to meet.

Callback

In week 44, Roman built tornado charts and break-evens for a project. Today's examples are the same tool applied to you. Find the currency move and the market fall that take your equity to zero, and the smaller ones that take you below your liquidity floor. Those two break-evens are the most important numbers on your personal balance sheet, and most wealthy people have never calculated them.

Recap

Currency mismatch and concentration change what your assets are worth to you, and leverage multiplies both. Measure net worth in the currency you spend, match debt and reserves to income, set a written concentration limit and run a combined stress case every year.

Next: Tessa, on The Rules: what happens, in law, when someone dies without an estate plan.
checklist: I report my net worth in one reporting currency.
I keep a currency table showing my net position in each currency.
Every loan is matched, where possible, to the currency of the income that repays it.
My emergency reserves are held in the currency of the obligations they cover.
I know my concentration ratio and my total personal leverage.
I have run a combined market and currency stress case this year.
I know the market fall and the currency move that would breach my liquidity floor.
I take hedging and refinancing decisions only with a licensed adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, currency mismatch and concentration can halve your net worth without a tenant leaving. If a building is valued in one currency and the loan is in another, a 25 percent currency fall can wipe out more than half the equity once leverage is applied. Borrow in the building's own currency and the same move costs a quarter. Concentration works the same way: put 80 percent of your assets in one market with half of them borrowed, and a 30 percent fall takes nearly half your equity. So I report net worth in the currency I spend, with a table of my net position in every other currency. I match debt and reserves to the income and spending they serve. I set a written maximum for any single exposure. And once a year I run a combined case, market and currency falling together, against my liquidity floor. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Reporting currency — the single currency in which you measure and compare your whole net worth, normally the one you spend.
Net open position — the asset value in a currency less the debt in that same currency, which gains or loses as the exchange rate moves.
Concentration ratio — the largest single exposure divided by total assets.

hostile.q: You are guaranteeing a loan in our currency, but most of your net worth is in another. What happens to your guarantee if that currency falls 30 percent?
hostile.a: I have run that case. On my current numbers a 30 percent fall reduces my net worth in your currency by a stated amount, which I can show you, and I still hold a liquidity reserve in your currency that covers the guarantee's realistic call. I do not rely on the foreign assets to meet it. I can give you the currency table and the stress case, and update them each year.

title: Dying Without a Plan: What the Law Does Instead
summary: If you die without a valid will, or become incapable without powers of attorney, the law does not leave a gap. It fills it with default rules you did not choose, a court process that takes time, and administrators you did not appoint. This lesson explains those defaults in concept and what a plan replaces.
body:
The law never leaves an estate without a plan. If you do not write one, it supplies a default: a statutory list of heirs, a court-appointed administrator and a public process, none of which you chose, and none of which knows your business.

Recall

Q. In personal tax, what is a deemed disposition at death, in concept?

A. A rule in some tax systems that treats a person as having sold their assets at market value immediately before death, so that accrued gains are taxed then. Whether and how it applies depends on the jurisdiction; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is the purpose of a family office's adviser review?

A. To test each adviser's fees, performance, conflicts and scope against written expectations at a fixed interval, so that a relationship continues because it earns its place and not out of habit.

Q. Who owns a key-person policy, and who receives the proceeds?

A. Usually the company owns it and receives the proceeds, because the company bears the loss. The tax treatment of premiums and proceeds is jurisdiction-specific and needs advice.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer's estate is harder to administer than most. It holds shares in private companies, interests in partnerships, guarantees, deposits held for buyers, projects mid-construction, and assets in more than one country. A default process designed for a house, a car and a bank account handles that badly. The cost is not only legal fees. It is the months in which nobody has clear authority to sign a draw, vote the shares, answer the lender or pay the contractor.

Dying without a will

In plain English: if you die without a valid will, you are said to die intestate. The law of the relevant place then sets out who inherits, usually in a fixed order of relatives such as a spouse, children, parents and siblings, and in fixed shares. It does not ask who you would have chosen, who is capable, or whether one heir should run the business.

The professional framing has two parts. First, distribution: intestacy rules decide who receives the estate, and the details differ between jurisdictions, including how a spouse, a former spouse, a common-law partner, stepchildren and children of earlier relationships are treated. Second, administration: someone must collect the assets, pay the debts and distribute what is left. With a will, you name that person, the executor. Without one, a court appoints an administrator, often after applications by relatives who may not agree with one another. Verify every one of these points against the law of each place where you hold assets before you rely on it.

A real example of scale. The musician Prince died in April 2016, and no will was found. A court had to appoint administrators, the question of who his legal heirs were had to be decided, and the estate took years to resolve, much of it involving the value of assets such as music rights that are hard to price. The lesson is not about celebrity. It is that an estate with complex, hard-to-value assets and no instructions becomes a long, expensive, public process.

Say that out loud now.

If I do not write the plan, the law writes one for me, and it does not know my business.

Becoming incapable without powers of attorney

The more common gap is not death but incapacity. If you are alive but unable to manage your affairs after an accident or illness, a will does nothing, because a will only speaks at death. The document that matters is a power of attorney: a written authority for a person you choose to act for you. Many systems distinguish one covering property and finances from one covering personal care and health decisions, and some require a specific form for it to survive your incapacity.

Without one, a relative may have to apply to a court to be appointed guardian or similar, which takes time, costs money and may produce someone you would not have chosen.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer is the sole director and signing officer of the company that owns a project under construction. He is in hospital for three months and cannot communicate. The lender's next draw needs a signed certificate. The contractor needs a change order approved. Nobody else holds signing authority, because the company's resolutions name only him, and he has no power of attorney. The draw stops, the contractor slows, and interest keeps running on the reserve. The fix was two documents and a board resolution naming an alternate signing officer. Note the distinction: a personal power of attorney may not let someone act as a company director, because the company's own constitution and corporate law govern that. Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer and estate lawyer.

Assets in several countries

Each country generally applies its own rules to assets located there, especially land. A will made in one place may be valid, partly valid or awkward to prove in another, so a second grant of authority, sometimes called ancillary probate, may be needed. Some planners use separate wills for separate jurisdictions, drafted so that one does not accidentally revoke the other. Week 92 covered this in depth. The point today is that a single will, written for one country, may not be a complete plan for an estate that crosses borders.

Second worked example, hypothetical. An estate holds a 2,000,000 dollar building in country A, a 1,000,000 dollar bank account in country B, and shares in a project company incorporated in country C. One will exists, made in country A. The executor proves it in A within months. The bank in B will not release funds until it sees a grant it recognises. The registrar in C will not transfer the shares until the company's own articles and C's procedure are satisfied. Three processes, three sets of fees, three timetables, and the slowest one decides when the family has access to the money.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the gap in authority, not the tax. For months nobody can lawfully act, and in a development business that means missed draws, defaulted covenants, stalled sites and forced sales. The control is a current will in each relevant jurisdiction, financial and personal-care powers of attorney, company resolutions naming an alternate signatory, and an asset map that tells your executor where everything is. Professional sign-off required: estate lawyer in each jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a will is enough. It covers death but not incapacity, it may not work outside the country where it was made, and it does not override the company's own signing rules or a shareholders' agreement. A second mistake is writing the will once and never reviewing it, so it still names an executor who has moved away and leaves assets you sold years ago.

A third mistake is forgetting the assets that pass outside the will. In many systems, insurance policies, some registered or retirement accounts and jointly held property can pass directly to a named beneficiary or a surviving joint owner, whatever the will says. If those designations are years out of date, the will and the designations can point in opposite directions, and in many systems the designation prevails; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Check every beneficiary designation when you check the will.

Callback

In week 8, Tessa and Warrick introduced the will, powers of attorney and insurance as the base of a plan. In week 69, JAX taught the death, disability and divorce clauses in a partner agreement. Put them together: your estate documents decide who receives your shares, but the partner agreement may decide whether they can keep them, sell them or vote them. The two must be read side by side.

Recap

Without a will, the law decides who inherits and a court appoints an administrator. Without powers of attorney, nobody can act for you if you are incapable. With assets in several countries, one will may not be enough. The cure is a short set of documents, kept current and kept consistent with your company records.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a currency loss from a finished balance sheet.
checklist: I have a current, valid will.
I have a will, or confirmed advice, for each jurisdiction where I hold assets.
I have a financial power of attorney and a personal-care power of attorney.
Each company I control has resolutions naming an alternate signing officer.
My estate documents and my partner agreements have been read side by side.
My executor knows where the original documents and the asset map are kept.
I review my estate documents at least once a year and after any major change.
Professional sign-off from an estate lawyer in each jurisdiction is on file.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the law never leaves an estate without a plan. If you die without a valid will, statutory rules decide who inherits, in fixed shares, and a court appoints an administrator you did not choose. That process is slow, costly and often public, and it was not designed for private company shares, guarantees and projects under construction. The bigger gap is incapacity. A will only speaks at death, so if you are alive but cannot act, you need powers of attorney for property and for personal care. And because a personal power of attorney may not let anyone act as a company director, each company needs resolutions naming an alternate signatory. With assets in several countries, one will may not be enough. The plan is a short set of documents: wills, powers of attorney, company resolutions and an asset map, kept current. Professional sign-off from an estate lawyer is required.
terms: Intestacy — dying without a valid will, so the law's default rules decide who inherits.
Power of attorney — a written authority that lets a chosen person act for you, including, if properly made, when you are incapable.
Ancillary probate — a second grant of authority needed to deal with an estate's assets in another jurisdiction.

hostile.q: You are the only signing officer of the borrower. If you are in hospital for three months, who signs my draw certificates?
hostile.a: The company has resolutions naming an alternate signing officer with stated limits, and I can give you certified copies. I also hold financial and personal-care powers of attorney, and my estate documents are consistent with the shareholders' agreement. If you want the alternate added to your list of authorised signatories now, we will do it before first draw.

title: Reverse Engineering a Currency Loss
summary: We start from a finished, hypothetical result: a property that rose 20 percent in its own currency, owned by an investor whose equity fell 45 percent. Working backward splits the loss into price, currency and debt, then sizes what a matched loan and a concentration limit would have saved.
body:
A building can rise in value and still lose you money. Work backward from the finished result and the loss splits cleanly into three parts: what the market did, what the currency did and what the debt did. Only one of those was a market risk; the other two were choices.

Recall

Q. Name the four quiet faults that destroy personal wealth.

A. Currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan. They look separate in calm years and arrive together in a crisis.

Q. In a family office, what is a liquidity floor?

A. A written minimum of cash and near-cash, in the currency of your obligations, that you will not invest or pledge, sized to cover a defined period of spending and contingent calls such as guarantees.

Q. What is the difference between term and permanent life insurance, in concept?

A. Term covers a fixed period and pays only if you die within it. Permanent coverage lasts for life and usually builds a cash value, at a much higher premium. Which suits you is a question for a licensed adviser.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer. When a result is bad, the first instinct is to blame the market. That is often wrong, and it teaches the wrong lesson. If you can take a finished result apart and price each cause, you learn which risks were bad luck and which were bad design, and you stop repeating the design.

The finished outcome

All figures are hypothetical round numbers. An investor spends in currency H. Ten years ago he bought a building in another country, valued in currency F. Today he receives a report.

The building rose 20 percent in its own currency. His equity in the building, measured in H, fell 45 percent, from 4,000,000 H to 2,200,000 H. He wants to know how a rising building produced a falling fortune.

Working backward, step by step

Step 1. Write down the end state. Equity today is 2,200,000 H. Equity at purchase was 4,000,000 H. The change is minus 1,800,000 H.

Step 2. Find the opening position. At purchase, the exchange rate was 1 F to 1.00 H. The building cost 10,000,000 F, which was 10,000,000 H. He borrowed 6,000,000 H, in his home currency, because the rate was cheaper. Equity was 10,000,000 less 6,000,000, which is 4,000,000 H.

Step 3. Find the closing position. The building is now worth 12,000,000 F, which is the 20 percent rise. The exchange rate is now 1 F to 0.60 H, meaning currency F fell 40 percent against H. In H, the building is worth 12,000,000 times 0.60, which is 7,200,000 H. The loan has been paid down to 5,000,000 H. Equity is 7,200,000 less 5,000,000, which is 2,200,000 H. That matches the report.

Step 4. Split the building's change into price and currency. The building's value in H moved from 10,000,000 to 7,200,000, a change of minus 2,800,000 H. Price effect, at the old exchange rate: the 2,000,000 F rise times 1.00 is plus 2,000,000 H. Currency effect, on today's value: 12,000,000 F times the change in rate, 0.60 less 1.00, is minus 4,800,000 H. Check: plus 2,000,000 and minus 4,800,000 is minus 2,800,000 H. It reconciles.

Step 5. Add the debt. Paying the loan down from 6,000,000 to 5,000,000 H added 1,000,000 H to equity. So the full bridge is: price plus 2,000,000, currency minus 4,800,000, debt repayment plus 1,000,000. Total minus 1,800,000 H. Every dollar of the loss is now explained.

Say that out loud now.

The market gave me 2,000,000. The currency took 4,800,000. The currency risk was a choice I made on the day I chose the loan.

Pricing the alternative

Step 6. Rebuild the deal with a matched loan. Suppose he had borrowed 6,000,000 F instead, in the building's currency, and paid it down to 5,000,000 F. Today that debt is 5,000,000 F times 0.60, which is 3,000,000 H. Equity is 7,200,000 less 3,000,000, which is 4,200,000 H, a gain of 200,000 H, or 5 percent. The mismatch cost 4,200,000 less 2,200,000, which is 2,000,000 H.

Notice what the matched loan does and does not do. It does not remove currency risk. The building is still worth less in H than it would be at the old rate. It removes the currency risk on the borrowed part, so only his own equity is exposed. A matched loan may carry a higher interest rate, and comparing that cost with the protection is the real decision. Ratios and loan terms here are commercial practice, not standards.

Step 7. Find the break-evens. With the mismatched loan, how far could F fall before equity dropped below the opening 4,000,000 H? Equity of 4,000,000 with debt of 5,000,000 needs a building worth 9,000,000 H. That needs a rate of 9,000,000 divided by 12,000,000, which is 0.75. So a fall of 25 percent was the break-even. How far before equity reached zero? A building worth 5,000,000 H needs a rate of 5,000,000 divided by 12,000,000, about 0.42, a fall of about 58 percent. Those two numbers belong on the first page of the original investment memo.

Step 8. Check what the bridge leaves out. This bridge measures equity in the building only. It ignores ten years of rent, which was also paid in F and therefore also shrank in H as the currency fell, and it ignores the interest paid. A full bridge adds net rent received and interest paid, each converted at the rate on the day it moved, plus fees and any tax. The method is unchanged; there are just more lines. If the full bridge does not reconcile to the bank statements, find the missing line before drawing any conclusion.

Second example: the concentration that broke the floor

Another hypothetical finished outcome. An investor's personal statement shows total assets of 10,000,000 dollars, debt of 4,000,000 and equity of 6,000,000 before a downturn. His written rule says equity must stay at or above 4,000,000 after a severe case of a 40 percent fall in his largest market. After the downturn, equity is 2,800,000. The rule broke. Why?

Work back. Equity fell by 3,200,000. If the whole loss came from one market falling 40 percent, the exposure was 3,200,000 divided by 0.40, which is 8,000,000 dollars, 80 percent of total assets. Now solve for the limit he should have had. The largest loss his rule allowed was 6,000,000 less 4,000,000, which is 2,000,000. At a 40 percent fall, that allows an exposure of 2,000,000 divided by 0.40, which is 5,000,000 dollars, 50 percent of assets. His rule implied a concentration limit of 50 percent. He never wrote it as one, so he never noticed he was at 80.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reading a bad result as one number and drawing the wrong lesson from it. The control is the bridge: open, close, price, currency, debt, fees, each reconciled to the last dollar, and each tagged as a market outcome or a design choice. A licensed adviser is required before you change a hedge, a loan or an allocation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares values in the asset's own currency and celebrates. Twenty percent up in F felt like success. The family spends H. Always restate the result in the currency you spend, and always show the currency effect as its own line.

Callback

In week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information: the implied land price and return. Today is the same method turned on yourself. In both cases you start from a number you can see and work back to the decisions you cannot, and in both cases the bridge must reconcile, or you have not understood it.

Recap

A building rose 20 percent and equity fell 45 percent. The bridge showed plus 2,000,000 from price, minus 4,800,000 from currency and plus 1,000,000 from repayment. A matched loan would have saved 2,000,000, and a written 50 percent concentration limit would have held the floor in the second case.

Next: Roman, on The Room: questioning a wealth manager about custody before you hand over a dollar.
checklist: I restate every result in the currency I spend.
I build a bridge from opening to closing equity that reconciles to the last dollar.
I show price, currency, debt and fees as separate lines.
I tag each line as a market outcome or a design choice.
I calculate the currency break-even before choosing a loan currency.
I convert my liquidity-floor rule into an explicit concentration limit.
I compare the cost of a matched loan with the protection it gives.
I make hedge and allocation changes only with a licensed adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, a building can rise and still lose you money. In our hypothetical case, a building went up 20 percent in its own currency, but the owner's equity fell 45 percent in the currency his family spends. Working backward, the bridge was: plus 2,000,000 from the local price rise, minus 4,800,000 from a 40 percent currency fall, and plus 1,000,000 from paying down the loan. The currency loss was a choice made on the day he borrowed in his home currency against a foreign asset. A matched loan would have saved 2,000,000. The break-even was a 25 percent currency fall, a number that belonged in the original memo. The second case showed a liquidity rule that implied a 50 percent concentration limit, while the investor sat at 80. So I build the bridge, reconcile it, and tag every line as market or design. A licensed adviser is required before I act.
terms: Equity bridge — a reconciliation from opening to closing equity that names every cause of the change.
Currency effect — the part of a change in value caused only by the exchange rate moving.
Break-even exchange rate — the rate at which equity returns to a stated level, such as its starting value or zero.

hostile.q: Your foreign asset rose 20 percent. Why does your personal statement show a loss?
hostile.a: Because I borrowed in my home currency and the asset's currency fell 40 percent. The bridge is: plus 2,000,000 from price, minus 4,800,000 from currency on the asset, plus 1,000,000 from repayment. The currency loss on the borrowed part was avoidable. Going forward, I match debt to the asset's currency where the extra interest cost is justified, and I report the currency effect as its own line.

title: The Custody Questions, Asked Calmly
summary: A polished wealth manager offers steady returns and asks you to open accounts with an affiliated firm. This lesson scripts the meeting: the questions that establish custody and independence, the lines never to say, the question behind the pitch, and how to stay composed when the answers get vague.
body:
The most valuable thing you can do in a meeting with someone who wants to manage your money is ask, calmly and early, who will hold it and who will check it. A good manager welcomes those questions. A bad one changes the subject.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 96?

A. Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties I can verify myself.

Q. In a family office, why separate the person who selects managers from the person who reports performance?

A. Because someone who chose a manager has a natural reluctance to report that the choice was poor. Separating the two keeps the reporting honest.

Q. What does a key-person policy do for a lender?

A. It gives the borrower cash if the person the deal depends on dies or is disabled, which can fund a replacement or repay debt, and some lenders ask for it as a condition.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as your wealth grows, people will seek you out to manage it. Most are honest. Some are excellent. A few are dangerous, and they are rarely the ones who look it. You cannot tell them apart by charm or by credentials. You can tell them apart by how they answer five plain questions about custody and verification, and by whether you have the composure to ask them.

The scene

This is a composite example. A manager, introduced by a respected acquaintance, meets you in a quiet office. His fund reports steady returns, very few losing months and a waiting list. He suggests you open accounts through a brokerage firm affiliated with his group, because it makes reporting simpler, and offers to send you a monthly statement himself. He says the strategy is proprietary, so detailed holdings are not shared, but you will be impressed by the results.

The lines to say

Open with your purpose, so the questions feel like process rather than suspicion: "Before we talk about returns, I go through the same custody questions with every manager. It is how I work."

Then the five questions, one at a time, with a pause after each.

"Who is the custodian, and is it independent of your firm?"

"Will the custodian send statements directly to me, and can I log in to the custodian's own system?"

"Who is the fund administrator, and who appoints and pays it?"

"Who audits the fund, and may I contact the audit partner to confirm the engagement?"

"What is the strategy, in a form I can check? I do not need your edge; I need to understand where the returns could come from and what would make them negative."

Close with a commitment you can keep: "Please send those answers in writing. I will review them with my adviser and come back to you by Friday."

Say that out loud now.

Before we talk about returns, I go through the same custody questions with every manager.

The lines never to say

"I trust you." It closes the inquiry and tells him you will not check.

"Everyone I know is in." It tells him your decision rests on social proof, which is the weakest evidence available.

"How much can I get in?" It tells him scarcity has worked on you, and it hands him the negotiation.

"I am not a numbers person." You are, and saying otherwise invites him to stop explaining.

The question behind the question

When he says the affiliated brokerage makes reporting simpler, the question behind it is whether he wants to control what you see. Simplicity for the manager often means a single source of information for you. When he says the strategy is proprietary, the question behind it is whether there is any strategy at all. A legitimate manager can describe the kind of risk he takes without giving away the specifics. When he mentions a waiting list, the question behind it is urgency: he would like you to decide before you check.

Roman's practice is to answer that urgency with time. A real opportunity survives a week of diligence. A pitch that cannot survive a week is telling you something.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after each custody question. The first answer, before he has decided what you want to hear, is the most honest. If the answer is vague, do not fill the silence with a suggestion. Let him either clarify or keep talking. Vagueness under a simple question is data.

Stay silent, too, after he names the returns. Do not react with enthusiasm. A neutral face keeps the conversation on evidence.

Holding your state

These questions can feel rude to ask a respected person, and the discomfort is physical: a warm face, a quickened pulse, an urge to soften. Name it to yourself as the feeling of doing diligence, not of being impolite. Slow your speech and lower your pace on the five questions. Write the answers down as he speaks, which gives your hands and eyes something steady to do and signals that the answers will be checked. If you notice yourself rushing, pause and look at your notes before the next question.

Two worked moments

First moment. You ask who the custodian is. He replies, "Our affiliate holds everything, but it is fully regulated." You write it down and say: "Thank you. Is there an independent custodian above the affiliate, or is the affiliate the only one?" If the affiliate is the only custodian, you have found the structure Rule 96 forbids, and the meeting has done its job.

Second moment, hypothetical numbers. He suggests a starting allocation of 2,000,000 dollars. Your written concentration rule caps any single manager at 10 percent of a hypothetical 8,000,000 dollar net worth, which is 800,000 dollars. You say: "My rule for any single manager is a fixed share of net worth. If we proceed, it will be within that limit, and only after the custody answers check out." You have stated a limit, not a negotiation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the respected introducer does your diligence for you, in your head. You assume that because a trusted person invested, the questions have been asked. They may not have been. The control is to ask the same five questions of every manager, in writing, whatever the introduction, and to confirm the answers with the custodian and auditor directly.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner asks about returns first and custody last, if at all. By the time custody comes up, he is already emotionally invested in the returns. Ask the plumbing questions first, while you are still neutral.

Callback

In week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the line "I will confirm by Friday". Today you are the one asking hard questions, and the same discipline applies in reverse. Ask once, clearly, pause, write the answer, and commit to a time when you will respond.

Family, legacy and what "enough" means

A manager's pitch works best on someone who has not decided what the money is for. If you do not know what enough looks like, every promise of more sounds like a reason to take more risk. So here is a question for you to answer in your own words, not mine: what would your family's life look like if you never made another dollar, and would that be enough?

Write the answer down and date it. Then ask whether your current concentration and custody arrangements protect that picture, or put it at risk for returns you may not need.

Recap

Ask the five custody questions first, calmly, pausing after each, and get the answers in writing. Never say you trust him or that everyone is in. Answer urgency with time, and keep any allocation inside your written limit.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: the week's six questions and Cole's Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I ask custody questions before I discuss returns.
I ask who the custodian is and whether it is independent.
I ask for direct statements and access to the custodian's own system.
I ask who the administrator and auditor are, and I confirm with them.
I ask for the strategy in a form I can check.
I never say I trust a manager or that everyone is in.
I keep any allocation within my written limit for a single manager.
I answer urgency with time and commit to a response date.
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, when someone wants to manage your money, ask early and calmly who will hold it and who will check it. Open with process: I ask the same custody questions of every manager. Then five questions, with a pause after each. Who is the custodian, and is it independent? Will it send statements directly to me? Who is the administrator? Who audits the fund, and may I confirm with them? What is the strategy, in a form I can check? Write the answers down and ask for them in writing. Never say I trust you, everyone I know is in, or how much can I get in. Behind a pitch for simplicity is a wish to control what you see; behind a waiting list is urgency. Answer urgency with time. Keep any allocation inside your written limit, and commit to a response by Friday.
terms: Introducer — a trusted person who brings you to a manager or deal, whose endorsement can wrongly replace your own diligence.
Fund auditor — an independent accounting firm that examines and gives an opinion on a fund's financial statements.
Social proof — the tendency to treat other people's choices as evidence that a choice is sound.

hostile.q: Everyone in this room has invested with me for years. Why are you asking about custody as if I were a stranger?
hostile.a: Because I ask every manager the same questions, including the ones I already respect. It is not about you; it is how I protect my family and keep my own rules. If the custody and audit arrangements are what you describe, the answers will take you a few minutes, and I will come back to you by Friday.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 96 Review: The Post-Mortem of a Personal Fortune
summary: Six questions on currency mismatch, concentration, custody and dying without a plan, a recap of the week, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical manager's statement, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: wealth is lost through its architecture more often than through its investments, so test the currency, the concentration, the custody and the estate plan together, before a crisis tests them for you.

Recall

Q. What is a net open position in a currency?

A. The value of your assets in that currency less your debts in the same currency. It gains or loses as the exchange rate moves.

Q. What should a family office investment policy statement say about liquidity?

A. The minimum held in cash and near-cash, the currency it is held in, what it must cover and for how long, and who may authorise drawing on it.

Q. Why review insurance coverage when a large guarantee is signed?

A. Because the guarantee is a contingent debt your family could inherit, and life or disability coverage may need to rise to cover a realistic call on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a post-mortem week is only useful if the lessons become habits. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer. If you hesitate, go back to that day's lesson tonight.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four quiet faults that destroy personal wealth, and say why they are dangerous together.

Answer: Currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan. They are dangerous together because the same crisis that drops a currency also drops local property, tightens local banks, exposes weak managers and coincides with personal stress, so they become correlated exactly when you need them not to be.

Question 2. Why did the Madoff fraud survive for so long?

Answer: Because one firm managed the money, held it and produced the statements, so there was no independent record to compare against. Investors accepted smooth returns, a famous name, a very small auditor and secrecy, and assumed someone else had checked.

Question 3. State Rule 96.

Answer: Never let the person who manages my money also hold it and report on it. Custody, administration and audit sit with independent parties I can verify myself.

Question 4. How does leverage change the effect of a currency fall on your equity?

Answer: It multiplies it. If the asset is in one currency and the debt in another, the whole asset value falls with the currency while the debt does not, so a 25 percent currency fall can remove far more than 25 percent of equity. Matching the debt to the asset's currency limits the exposure to your own equity.

Question 5. What does the law do if you die without a will, and what is the larger gap a will does not cover?

Answer: Default intestacy rules decide who inherits and a court appoints an administrator. The larger gap is incapacity: a will only speaks at death, so you need powers of attorney, and company resolutions naming an alternate signing officer.

Question 6. In a meeting with a new manager, which questions come first, and why?

Answer: The custody questions: who the custodian is, whether statements come directly to you, who the administrator and auditor are, and what the strategy is in a form you can check. They come first because once you are excited about returns, you are less likely to ask them.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ford framed the four quiet faults and why they arrive together. Ford and Roman took the Madoff fraud through seven steps, giving Rule 96 on independent custody. Roman priced currency mismatch and concentration on a personal balance sheet, with Warrick's ledger. Tessa explained the law's default plan for someone who dies or becomes incapable without one. Roman reverse engineered a currency loss into price, currency and debt. And Roman ran the custody meeting with a polished manager.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 96 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair. Read this hypothetical quarterly statement as a hostile auditor would, and find the defects before reading on.

Quarterly Client Report, prepared by Steady Growth Advisers. Account value at quarter end: 2,400,000 dollars, up 2.1 percent, our 31st consecutive positive quarter. Holdings are maintained by our affiliate, Steady Growth Securities, on your behalf; a separate custodian statement is not required. Positions are summarised by strategy rather than by security to protect our proprietary approach. Valuations are prepared by our in-house team. The fund's financial statements are audited annually by a firm engaged by the manager. Your next allocation window closes in ten days; existing clients receive priority.

The defects. First, custody sits with the manager's own affiliate, and the report says no separate custodian statement is needed, which removes the one independent check. Second, 31 consecutive positive quarters is a return stream too smooth to accept without a strong explanation. Third, holdings are shown by strategy, not by security, so nothing can be confirmed against an exchange or a custodian. Fourth, valuations are in-house, with no independent administrator. Fifth, the auditor is unnamed and engaged by the manager, so you cannot confirm the engagement or the firm's standing. Sixth, the closing allocation window applies urgency at the moment you should be slowing down. Seventh, the report gives no fees, so you cannot see what the 2.1 percent cost you.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence that would cure each defect, and that list is the real lesson. An independent custodian's statement in your name, received directly. A holdings list by security. A named independent administrator's valuation. The audit firm's name and a direct confirmation from the audit partner. A written explanation of where the returns could come from and what would make them negative. A full fee schedule. If the manager cannot produce these within a week, Rule 96 decides the matter.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "We both do well on our projects. Why spend time on how our personal wealth is held?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because fortunes are usually lost through their structure, not their investments. There are four faults to watch. Currency mismatch: if our assets are in one currency and our debts or family spending in another, a currency move can take far more than its own percentage once leverage is involved, so we match debt and reserves to income. Concentration: one market, bank or partner carrying most of our net worth, so we write a maximum share and stick to it. Custody: whoever manages our money must not also hold it and report on it; we want an independent custodian, administrator and auditor, and we check directly. And estate planning: without wills and powers of attorney, the law appoints people we did not choose and nobody can sign for our companies if we are ill. Once a year we stress all four together, because in a crisis they arrive together. A licensed adviser is required before we change anything."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after a week like this is agreeing with every lesson and changing nothing. The control is to pick one fault, the one your own balance sheet shows most clearly, and fix it before next week's checkpoint.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the four faults as a checklist to tick once. They are a review to repeat. Currencies move, positions grow, managers change and families change, so a structure that was sound last year can be unsound now.

Callback

In week 2, Kema and Ford introduced the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed, then explain why. This week is the same tool applied to a fortune. Imagine your family's wealth has been badly damaged ten years from now. The most likely explanations are on this page.

Recap

Four faults, tested together; Rule 96 on independent custody; currency and concentration priced with leverage; the law's default estate plan; a reconciled bridge; and five calm custody questions. Next week is the checkpoint for this phase.

speak: Mr Shabazz, this week's lesson is that fortunes are lost through architecture more often than through investments. Four faults do the damage: currency mismatch, concentration, unsafe custody and no estate plan, and in a crisis they arrive together. hostile.q: You have described four risks. Which one is the largest on your own balance sheet today, and what are you doing about it?
hostile.a: Concentration. Most of my net worth is in development equity in one market, which is normal for a developer but is my largest exposure. I have written a maximum share for any single project and market, I am building a liquidity reserve in the currency of my guarantees, and I review the position quarterly against that limit. A licensed adviser is reviewing the plan before I act.
